newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends near flat in quiet post-holiday US trade.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends near flat in quiet post-holiday US trade.

text.p: The dollar ended little changed on Thursday, sticking to narrow ranges against other major currencies in thin post-Christmas holiday trade.

Helped by a sharp decline in Japanese stocks and comparative strength in U.S. assets, the dollar jumped to a 44-month high against the Japanese yen in Asian trade. But with most major European markets closed for the Christmas holidays, U.S. trade was relatively subdued, dealers said.

"We're in holiday mode, it's very thin and there's very little incentive to be involved at this point unless you really have to be," said Paul Park, vice president and dollar/yen trader at Pittsburgh-based Mellon Bank.
The most active trading occured in Tokyo, where Japanese stocks slid amid growing concerns that the government's austere fiscal policies will hinder already anemic Japanese economic growth.
The Nikkei average of 225 leading Japanese shares dropped as low as 18,819.92 on Thursday, the first time it has fallen below the key 19,000 level since December 6, 1995.
The index clawed its way higher in late trade to end down 257.83 points at 19,291.58, nudging dollar/yen off a peak of 115.08, its highest level since April of 1993.

But dealers said they expect Japanese stock weakness to continue to weigh on the yen. The poor stock performance makes a near-term Japanese interest rate rise, which would tend to benefit the yen, increasingly unlikely.
"The dollar's rise against the yen came on the back of the drop in the Nikkei," said Mellon's Park.
"The knee-jerk reaction has just been to buy dollars against yen. It's the easiest money out there right now and I think it will continue to attract investors," he added.
The dollar ended at 114.88/98 yen, little changed from its opening level of 114.85/90 but up from Tuesday's close of 114.47.

Helping to cap the dollar's gains against the yen were comments from a senior Japanese Finance Ministry official, who told Reuters that Japan's monetary authorities did not welcome wild currency fluctuations and were keeping a close watch on developments in the foreign exchange market.
Dealers interpreted the remarks as a sign that Japanese officials would frown on a further decline in their currency against the dollar.
"With dollar/yen reaching new cycle highs it was enough to introduce a little bit of caution into the market," said Bob Lynch, senior currency analyst at MMS International.
Dealers said strength in the Dow Industrials, which rose about 24 points to end at 6547, was broadly supportive of the dollar on Thursday.
Nevertheless, thin holiday conditions confined the U.S. unit to extremely narrow ranges versus most major currencies.

The dollar ended at 1.5528/38 marks on Thursday, relatively unchanged from its opening of level of 1.5540/50 marks. And after setting a 29-month high of 1.3475 Swiss francs during Asian trade, the dollar settled at 1.3430/40 Swiss francs versus 1.3428/38 in early trade.
Elsewhere, the British pound was relatively flat at $1.6735/45 against $1.6750/60. The dollar fell slightly to Canadian $1.3635/40 from C$1.3639/44.
The Australian dollar ended at $0.7953/58 against an opening rate of $0.7951/58.
